rv.q: There were opportunities here to craft either a tighter thriller or a more penetrating character study; Street opts for something in-between, light on dramatic momentum but rich in biographical detail.
A Small And Quiet Light, Stephanie Street's warm, theatrical tribute to Khan, is so anxious to be respectful, it makes our heroine seem a little dull.
Noor’s courage shines through, but the woman herself remains an enigma, frustratingly out of reach, lost in the night and fog of war.
The most frustrating thing about the production is the lack of both dramatic conflict and the absence of danger, of real stomach-churning fear.
Unfortunately, this play managed neither for me.
A quietly devastating play, this reaches the silence of great writing from a great subject.
There’s a good idea in that, but in execution it’s frankly a bit of a muddle.
An engaging play about an admirable woman, with an all-female cast, a small and quiet light needs a little more grit to lift this dramatization out of the archive.

cn.t: Critics find this WWII drama about heroic agent Noor-un-Nisa Inayat Khan well-intentioned but dramatically uneven, with most agreeing the play struggles to capture its subject's complexity despite shining a light on an important untold story.
